planting.note: Transplant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in early spring into deep, fertile, well-drained soil with room for a wide-spreading canopy; fresh conker-like seeds can also be fall-sown or cold-stratified over winter for spring germination.

directions: Common horse chestnut is a large, round-headed European shade tree known for the upright, candle-like panicles of white flowers, each marked with a yellow-to-pink throat blotch, that cover the tree in late spring. Its big palmately compound leaves cast dense shade, and by autumn the leathery, spine-covered husks split open to release the glossy brown seeds (conkers) that children have long collected for games, though all parts of the tree are toxic if eaten. Plant in deep, moisture-retentive soil in full sun and allow generous room to grow, since the dense canopy and surface roots make underplanting difficult. In warm, humid summers the foliage is prone to leaf blotch and bleeding canker, so cooler-summer regions tend to show it at its best.

planting.note: This grafted, fully double-flowered selection is sterile and propagated only by grafting onto seedling rootstock, so start from a nursery tree set out in early spring in deep, well-drained soil.

directions: 'Baumannii' is a long-cultivated, fully double-flowered sporting of common horse chestnut, selected in Switzerland in the 1820s, that produces dense, pure white flower spikes lasting noticeably longer than the single-flowered species because the blooms never set seed. Because the flowers are sterile, the tree never develops the spiny fruit husks of the straight species, making it a tidier, less messy choice for lawns, parks, and streetscapes. It otherwise grows and flowers like the species, with the same broad canopy and palmate leaves, and is propagated exclusively by grafting since it sets no viable seed. Give it the same deep, fertile soil and full sun as the species.

planting.note: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with full sun; this Himalayan species flowers later than common horse chestnut, so it largely escapes damage from late spring frosts.

directions: Indian horse chestnut is a handsome Himalayan tree valued for flowering several weeks later than common horse chestnut, sending up tall, narrow candles of white flowers flushed with pink and yellow in mid- to late summer when few other large trees are in bloom. Its leaves are larger and glossier than those of the European species, with longer, more tapered leaflets that often emerge bronze-tinted before turning deep green. It wants the same deep, moisture-retentive soil as its European cousin but is somewhat less reliably hardy in the coldest zones and appreciates a site sheltered from harsh winter wind. Grow it as a specimen lawn or park tree where its late season of bloom and bold foliage can stand out.

planting.note: Set out in early spring in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil with ample overhead and root room, since this species eventually forms a very large, wide-canopied tree.

directions: Japanese horse chestnut is a stately forest tree from Japan's mountains, carrying some of the largest palmate leaves of any temperate tree, with individual leaflets reaching well over a foot long, and upright white flower panicles marked with a red-orange throat in late spring. In its native range the large seeds are leached and processed over days to remove bitter tannins and toxins before being pounded into a traditional starch for mochi and other foods, though raw seeds should never be eaten. It needs the same deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil as other horse chestnuts and is best reserved for large landscapes, parks, and arboreta where its eventual great size and coarse winter silhouette can be accommodated. Fall color is typically a warm orange-bronze.

planting.note: Transplant nursery stock in early spring into deep, fertile soil with full sun and plenty of room; seed requires a warm period followed by cold stratification and often does not germinate until its second spring.

directions: European ash is a large, fast-growing deciduous tree long important across its native range for strong, elastic timber used in tool handles, sports equipment, and furniture, and it holds deep cultural significance in Northern European folklore as the World Tree, Yggdrasil, of Norse mythology. It is easily identified in winter by its distinctive jet-black, velvety leaf buds set opposite one another on gray twigs, and by the pinnately compound leaves that emerge late in spring and drop while still green in fall. Plant in deep, fertile soil in full sun and give it room to reach a broad, open crown. Populations across Europe and increasingly in North American plantings have been devastated by ash dieback disease (Hymenoscyphus fraxineus) and emerald ash borer, so new plantings should be weighed carefully against local pest and disease pressure.

planting.note: Plant a grafted standard in early spring in full sun with deep, fertile soil, and stake the young trunk until the graft union is sturdy enough to carry the cascading crown.

directions: One of the oldest weeping tree selections still grown, 'Pendula' is a sport of European ash with strongly pendulous branches that cascade to the ground from a grafted head, forming a dense, tent-like canopy that can be walked beneath. It is usually trained as a single-trunk standard, grafted high, and allowed to form its own umbrella-shaped mound of weeping growth with little pruning beyond removing wayward upright shoots that occasionally revert toward the ungrafted species. The pinnate leaves and black winter buds are identical to the straight species, but the strongly weeping habit makes it a dramatic specimen for large lawns where a shaded, enclosed space beneath the canopy is wanted. It shares the species' vulnerability to ash dieback and emerald ash borer where those pests are established.

planting.note: Plant grafted nursery stock in early spring in full sun with deep, fertile soil; site it where the winter stem color and fall foliage will be backlit or viewed against a dark evergreen backdrop.

directions: 'Jaspidea' is a long-established golden-stemmed selection of European ash, grown chiefly for its bright yellow young shoots and twigs that glow in low winter light, and for a reliable clear butter-yellow fall foliage color that is showier than the typical species, which often drops its leaves green. Through the growing season it behaves much like the straight species, forming a large, open-crowned deciduous tree with the same black winter buds and pinnately compound leaves, so it needs the same deep, fertile soil and sunny, open site. It is most effective planted where the winter twig color can be appreciated at a distance, such as across a lawn or lake, and like the species it is vulnerable to ash dieback and emerald ash borer where those pests occur.

planting.note: Set out seedlings well after all frost danger in humid, warm, frost-free conditions; araza needs consistently high humidity and shelter from wind and cannot tolerate any frost.

directions: Araza is a small, shrubby tree native to the Peruvian and Brazilian Amazon, grown for its bright yellow, downy-skinned, globe- to pear-shaped fruit with intensely acidic, aromatic pulp that is almost never eaten fresh but is prized throughout the Amazon basin for juice, jam, ice cream, and dessert sauces once sweetened. It flowers and fruits within a couple of years of planting and can bear more than once a year in consistently warm, humid climates. Grow it in rich, moist, well-drained soil with shelter from wind and from the intense midday sun, since it is naturally an understory tree of humid lowland rainforest and resents dry air or cold. Outside the humid tropics it is really only practical as a large container or greenhouse specimen.
